en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of the Great Master Gaofeng When I first began to study the Buddhist scriptures, I obtained several volumes of sutras, treatises, and miscellaneous writings from both ancient and modern times. Among them were the words of the Great Master;

I was filled with joy and accepted them with faith, as if encountering a torch in the darkness—a feeling that remains unchanged to this day. This is because, throughout my lifelong investigation of the Dharma...
This matter is most extremely sharp and keen; none surpasses the Master. It is truly as if forged from pure steel.
Each time one unrolls and reads it, one’s human spirit is stirred and inspired, causing one to leap with joy, temper oneself, and forget weariness.

Although its realization is profound and mysterious, one dares not fathom it with ordinary conjecture; rather, one simply perceives its direct root-source, which sheds all conceptual molds. Recently...
The spirit of Ciming Miaoxi is far-reaching; he does not fall short of the venerable elders Deshan and Linji. How magnificent! How grand!
He may truly be called a banner of light illuminating the Dharma-ending age. My only regret was that the Tripitaka had not yet included his works and that printed editions were still scarce;
for thirty years, this has weighed heavily upon my heart. Now, I have once again had these old manuscripts carved into woodblocks for publication.
Yet among the practitioners of the Lotus Society, there were those who looked at one another and whispered, "He causes the myriad streams to swirl about and points them toward the Pure Land;
why then does he again so earnestly praise this compilation? Does it mean that recollecting Amitābha Buddha is not as good as observing the 'myriad dharmas returning to One'?
Consequently, they became agitated and stirred up a great commotion. Alas! It is sufficient simply to understand "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?"—there is no need for anything else.
Question: "Where does 'One' return? Now there is a person here who knows that I am his father, yet he further doubts from where his own body has come.

Upon hearing this, how could anyone not collapse in laughter? An ancient patriarch said: "It is like a person traveling a long distance; one sets reaching the destination as the goal, rather than taking the difficulties and ease along the way into account.
O virtuous ones, the gates of expedient means are many, but the path returning to the source is one. I pray you do not...
If you continue to harbor doubts and waste the passing years, you ought instead to go directly and hasten toward the plan for reaching home.
Once you have reached home, neither the thousand-fathom cliff nor the pool of seven treasures will be accepted by the wise host.
Recorded respectfully by Yunqi Zhuhong on a day of Buddha-joy in the year of Jihai, the twenty-seventh year of the Wanli era.
Compiled by his disciples for study from the Upper Volume of the Recorded Sayings of Great Master Gao Feng. Re-engraved by Hongli of Lingyin Monastery.
The Dharma Talks of Shuangji An in Huzhou.
In the spring of the Jiaxu year of the Xianchun era, the Master addressed the assembly at the hermitage, saying:

"To speak of the profound and the subtle, to discuss the nature and the mind—arranging flowers and clustering brocade, clever and novel, as numerous as hemp and millet—from antiquity until now, there has been nothing that is not thus."
This is a fellow who rides on empty space and responds to echoes; a spirit that leans upon grass and clings to wood.
Although this mountain monk is but a blade of grass grown in his house, I certainly will not hide my body here. Since it is so, tell me:
as you open the hall for the assembly today, what is the one phrase for issuing a brand-new set of regulations? He lets out a shout and says: "When the tally arrives, it is executed."
Addressing the assembly: There is a thing, vividly clear, which the Buddhas and patriarchs cannot see through; the whole earth knows no one who recognizes it.
It is always upon the tip of the tongue, yet one cannot spit it out no matter how hard one tries. Even if one could spit it out, it would still be like sipping broth from a sesame cake.
Addressing the assembly: There is a phrase, there is no phrase. The golden crow swallows the jade hare. Like a vine leaning against a tree; a mangy horse tied to a withered post.
When the tree falls, the vine unravels. Burned throughout the entire winter, it is not yet exhausted. Where does the phrase return? A stone tiger crouches in the middle of the road.
Hehe! Great laughter. A dragon’s head and a snake’s tail. Pressed down into the mire. A sharp blade does not slay one who is innocent. And so it is.
"Where does the fault lie in the Way of Mount Tiantong? He then let out a great laugh and descended from his seat. Addressing the assembly, he said:

"A thousand ridges and ten thousand mountains are covered in snow; the five lakes and four seas are frozen solid. The pure light forms a single expanse, and every single thing is luminous. Now tell me:
what about Zhaozhou’s 'cypress tree,' Yunmen’s 'dry turd,' and Dongshan’s 'three pounds of flax'? He finished.
What, after all, is this? [He lets out a shout] and says: "The morning star appears at midday; one still awaits the crowing of the dawn cock.
Addressing the assembly on New Year’s Day: "A spring New Year’s morn is hard to encounter in a hundred years; The young maiden’s makeup is more fresh and new than ever.
Only Old Wang the Second from the eastern village Remains as before, her face covered in dust."
Dissolving the retreat, he addresses the assembly: "For ninety days, we gripped the rope-tie so tightly that not even a hair’s breadth of movement was permitted;

it reached the point where every one of you had skin pierced through to the bone, scattered and broken apart. Looking at this with cold eyes, it is truly like digging through the earth to find the sky—a thousand errors, ten thousand mistakes.
Today, arriving here, I cannot help but let loose a single thread, so that both you and I may be free from restraint and constraint. East.
To the southwest, northwest, and northeast, they soar and drift spontaneously; in the heavens and among humans, they roam at ease and enjoy happiness. Although this is so, tell me:
should they suddenly encounter boiling cauldrons and glowing coals, or sword-trees and knife-mountains, where would you say they would find a place to settle? After a long silence, he said:
"Evil!
[The Master] addressed the assembly: "Ten thousand miles away, not a single cloud hangs; from within the void, a single aperture breaks forth.
The Double-Tufted Peak leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, while the staff raises its voice and shouts loudly at the crossroads. Now tell me, what is it he is shouting?"
"What is it? [The Master] struck the meditation seat with his whisk and said: "In the blazing heat of the sixth month, ice is born from fire;
at midnight, the sun's orb shines at noon. He addressed the assembly:
"Of the ninety days of this summer retreat, look—already half is gone. You who dwell in the face-gate beyond positions, quickly open your eyes!"
Look closely! Coldly, suddenly they meet. The red thread at the heels is severed; within the palm, one grasps the universe. Turning the body, one wanders through the azure void.
It is truly laughable that in years past, Old Ruiyan called out repeatedly upon the "Awakened Stone.
[He then raises his whisk and says: "O Assembly, is this the Master of Ruiyan? Or is it Linji’s 'Unpositioned True Person'?"
Yes. If you can truly emerge from this, I grant that your lifelong study of the Way is complete.
But if it is not yet so, he throws down his whisk and says: "Scatter it before the steps; calculate the account tomorrow morning."
Addressing the assembly: The spring colors of the Five Lakes are at their full bloom; this is precisely the time when merit is perfected and fruition is complete.

Jade butterflies pierce through flowers, scattering fragments of brocade; yellow orioles cast themselves upon willows, their tangled threads hanging down. Lingyun lost his mother-born eyes, and Beizhang added a double-furrowed brow.
Countless guests by the waterside and beneath the trees vainly attempt to cross Mount Sumeru with their bamboo staffs.

Addressing the assembly: The Buddhas of the three periods have not reached this in their preaching; yet as soon as they open their mouths, they hit upon it. The Patriarchs of successive generations have not reached this in their practice;
yet as soon as they move a step, they tread upon it. When both practice and preaching have reached it, what then? This is precisely the time to travel on pilgrimage.
Addressing the assembly on New Year’s Day: Last year this mountain monk was thirty-six; this year he has added another year. This is known to everyone.
[He] picks up his staff and says, "Tell me, how old is this staff? [He] strikes the meditation seat and says, "The new year begins its reign;
all things are renewed."
Addressing the assembly, he raised the case of Nanquan’s public announcement: "Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, last night at the third watch, gave rise to views of Buddha and views of Dharma;
each was given twenty blows and banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains. This was entirely true. Zhaozhou then stepped forward and said:
“Whom does the staff strike? Nanquan said, “Where does the fault lie? A pair of unperforated iron hammers.
Baizhang then prostrated. Nanquan returned to his quarters; it was like adding further bitterness to the cries of heaven.

Although Master Nanquan possessed the eye atop his head and was clear in his judgments of reward and punishment, even upon close inspection, he was merely driving a stake into empty space. If not for...
Regarding Zhaozhou’s later words, I do not know how they are to be resolved. Peakong did not say so;
rather, if someone were suddenly to give rise to views of Buddha or views of Dharma, he would simply say to them: "Excellent, excellent! When the time comes, the principle will manifest of itself."

Addressing the assembly: "The hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, the patriarchs of successive generations, and even the old monks throughout the land—all fall into this pit and this ditch at this very moment.
(He strikes the meditation seat once with his whisk. "Is there anyone who can leap out?
(He strikes it again once. "Three lives, sixty kalpas."
Addressing the assembly, he raised an example: Once, when Danxia was passing through a monastery, he encountered a freezing cold snap.
Upon entering the hall, he saw a wooden Buddha and took it up to burn as fuel. The monastery’s caretaker happened to see this and rebuked him, saying, "How can you burn my wooden Buddha?
Danxia used his staff to stir the ashes and said, "I am burning for its relics. The caretaker replied, "A wooden Buddha—how could it have relics? Danxia said, "Since there are none..."
"Śāriputra, please ask for two more statues so that we may burn them again. Thereafter, the abbot’s eyebrows and beard fell out. The Master commented:
"Danxia burned the wooden Buddha because he was driven by the cold; what else could it have been? Yet the abbot’s eyebrows and beard fell out."
"Occasionally forming words—what is there to doubt? If you try to deliberate upon this as if it were the Buddha-dharma, take it for granted that you will enter hell as fast as an arrow.
[He] threw down his whisk and descended from the seat.
Addressing the assembly: Guizong wiped away his eyes; the Second Patriarch calmed his mind by severing his arm; Yunmen pressed him until he broke a leg;
Xuansha smashed his toes with a mortar pestle. This lot of scavenging fellows—taking up the whisk, he said:
"Had I known there was such news as this, I would have spared seeing blood splattered all over the ground."

Addressing the assembly, he placed his staff across his shoulder and looked left and right, saying: "Does the great assembly understand? With my knotted staff slung over my shoulder, I do not look back at people;
I go straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks."
In the winter of the Dinghai year of the Zhizhi era (1297), the assembly requested Master Shi to open the hall at Shizi Chan Temple on Mount Xitianmu in Hangzhou.
He then proceeded to the Stone Chamber; having finished offering incense and making prayers for the Emperor, he spoke these words of dharma.
Next, he holds up the incense and says: "This single offering of incense does not depend on the sun and moon within a flask, nor is it the spring breeze beyond the kalpas.
Having encountered the lethal hand several times, it has become transparent and radiant from every side. Now that it is set down, the earth shakes with sixfold tremors;
yet when picked up, it fills and shatters empty space. But tell me, how is it when neither picked up nor set down?"

He gave a shout. He performed a woman’s bow and burned incense in the incense burner as an offering to the old monk who formerly resided at Mount Yangshan—one with horns, covered in fur, and lacking nostrils—to repay the kindness of the Dharma-milk. He then took his seat. A monk asked: "The ten directions gather together;
each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting the Buddha; with an empty mind, they return having passed the imperial examination. (Pang)
The layman said, "When you speak thus, Master, do you have any way of benefiting others? The Master replied, "I do. The layman pressed further, "Ultimately, which phrase is it?
The Master said, "Ask from the beginning. The layman asked, "What is 'the assembly gathered together from the ten directions'?"
The Master said: "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages are mixed together. The student asked: "What is it that each and every one studies as non-action?
The Master said: "The mouth swallows Buddhas and patriarchs; the eyes cover heaven and earth. The student asked: "What is the field for selecting Buddhas? The Master said:
"Ten thousand *li* from east to west, eight thousand *li* from south to north. The monk asked, "What is it like to return home having passed the examination with one's mind empty?
The Master said, "To move one’s countenance is to reveal the ancient path; do not fall into the trap of the silent mechanism.

The monk asked, "If that is so, then every word reveals the ultimate truth, and every sentence points toward the source. The Master said, "Where have you seen this? The monk gave a shout. The Master said, "This too is like swinging a club to strike at the moon."
The student said, "Let this matter rest for now. As for today’s gathering of the ten directions at Xifeng, where the Field for Selecting Buddhas is opened—what auspicious signs are there ultimately?
The Master replied, "The mountains, rivers, and great earth; the myriad phenomena in their dense array; sentient and insentient beings alike."
"All have already attained Buddhahood. The student asked, "Since all have already attained Buddhahood, why is it that this student has not?
The Master said, "If you were to attain Buddhahood, how could you cause the entire earth to attain Buddhahood? The student asked, "Ultimately, where does the student's fault lie?"
The Master said, "South of Xiang, north of Tan. The monk asked, "Do you still permit this student to repent? The Master said, "Prostrate yourself.
As soon as the monk bowed, the Master said, "A lion bites; a hound chases after clods of earth.

The Master then raised his whisk and called to the assembly, saying, "This is the field for selecting Buddhas; those who have emptied their minds return with the highest honors. Clever fellows—if you turn toward this..."
When you see this, you will see where Layman Pang establishes his body and sustains his life.
Once you see where Layman Pang establishes his body and sustains his life, you will see where the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past established their bodies and sustained their lives.

Once you see where the Buddhas and Patriarchs established their bodies and sustained their lives, you will see where you yourself establish your body and sustain your life. Once you see where you yourself establish your body and sustain your life...
In this state, there is no hindrance to breaking off your staff here, hanging up your alms-bag, and spending your days in leisure beneath the three rafters and before the seven-foot mat—
chewing rice that contains no grain, drinking broth that is not wet, and stretching out your legs to sleep. However,
if you cannot distinguish master from servant or differentiate beans from wheat, then with no other choice, you must press down the clouds and turn toward the midst of empty space.
I have written this "Upward to the Great Man" (Shang Daren) to teach all people how to paint a cat after the model.
In years past, when I was at Shuangjing, less than a month had passed since my return to the hall when, suddenly in the midst of sleep, I was struck by doubt: "All dharmas return to the One;
to what does the One return? From that moment on, my state of doubt arose all at once; I neglected sleep and forgot to eat, unable to distinguish east from west or day from night.
Whether dividing food, opening or unfolding one’s alms bowl, defecating or urinating, or even in every movement and stillness, every word and silence—it is all simply this:
"Where does it all return? There is not the slightest thought of difference, nor can even the slightest thought of difference arise;
it is just like being nailed down or glued, unable to be shaken or moved, even when amidst a vast and crowded multitude.
In the midst [of this state], there was not a single person who resembled him. From morning until evening, and from evening until morning, he remained limpid and profound, distinct and towering;
pure and clear, utterly free of a speck of defilement. A single thought spanned ten thousand years; the environment was still and people were forgotten.
He was as if dazed or as if a pillar, unaware that six days had passed. While following the assembly in chanting sutras at the Three Pagodas, he suddenly raised his head and beheld Wuzu Fayan.

A True Eulogy for the Abbot: Suddenly triggered by the old Master Yangshan’s question from days past regarding the phrase "dragging a corpse," it was as if empty space were pulverized and the great earth submerged;
subject and object were both forgotten, like a mirror reflecting a mirror.
From beginning to end, I silently brought up the "Wild Fox" of Baizhang, the "Buddha-nature of the Dog," the "Cheongju Robe," and the story of the Woman Emerging from Samādhi.
Upon examination, it was not at all clear. The wondrous function of Prajñā is truly not a falsehood. Regarding the "Mu" (No) koan I previously studied, nearly three years have passed;
except for the two meals of porridge and rice, I never once ascended the meditation cushion. Even when exhausted, I did not lean against anything.
Although I moved east and west day and night, I was constantly rolled into a single lump with the two demons of dullness and distraction, performing every possible trick.
The two [methods] were ineffective; over this "Mu" (無) character, I never once for even a brief moment managed to exert effort until it became a solid realization.
After I made my own resolution, I investigated the root of my illness and found there was no other cause: it was simply because I had not applied myself to the practice upon the ground of doubt.
I did nothing but "hold up" (the koan); while holding it up, it was present, but as soon as I stopped, it vanished. If I wished to give rise to doubt...

Furthermore, there is no place to apply one's hand; even if one were able to apply it and gain some degree of doubt, in a mere instant, one would inevitably be struck by dullness and distraction, splitting the matter into two pieces.
Thus, one would have wasted much time and endured much hardship in vain, making not the slightest progress.
Where would it all end? Moreover, this is different from the "Mu" (No) koan; rather, it is simply a matter of doubt.
Emotions arise easily; they appear at once without waiting for repeated reflection, deliberation, or intentional effort.

Once the spirit of inquiry (*yiqing*) has slightly coalesced into a mass, the mind that can act [upon delusions] ceases to exist. When this capacity to act no longer exists, what is contemplated is immediately forgotten.

This causes the myriad conditions to cease of their own accord without being suppressed, and the six sense-facets to become still of their own accord without being stilled. One does not commit even the slightest transgression.
Dust. Suddenly entering the samādhi of no-mind, when one unexpectedly encounters the place where porridge or rice is eaten, one will surely reach for the spoon and chopsticks by the side of the bowl.
One need not fear that the turtle will escape from the jar; this is a proven method that will certainly not deceive you.
If there were even a single word here that deluded people, I would personally incur the eternal fall of being ploughed with a tongue-pulling plow. For those currently studying...
Bodhisattvas of Prajñā must clearly understand this great matter. Disregarding the height of the mountains and the breadth of the waters, you have come specifically to see the Western Peak;
moreover, each of you has lit incense and candles, established precepts and vows, and sharpened your teeth and ground your jaws.
Firm your resolve with the fortitude of iron and stone. Having such principles and such insight, you must by all means not betray your own original aspiration;
do not betray the hearts of your parents who relinquished you to leave the household life; and do not betray the faith of the donors who have newly constructed this monastic hall.
Do not betray the protective heart of the king and the great ministers. Proceed directly with great faith; proceed directly without alteration;
proceed directly, standing like a ten-thousand-fathom cliff; proceed directly, painting a cat exactly as it is. Paint it, paint it again.

When painting reaches the point where the lines intersect in a lattice pattern, where the paths of consciousness are cut off, and where both person and phenomena are forgotten—suddenly, from the tip of the brush, a living cat leaps forth.
Aha! It turns out that the entire great earth is this very field for selecting Buddhas.
The entire earth is this very self. Reaching this point, what need is there to speak of Layman Pang? Even the Three Vehicles and the Ten Stages would lose heart and tremble;
even the blue-eyed one (Mañjuśrī) and the yellow-headed one (Vimalakīrti) would find no place to set foot.

Nevertheless, if you wish to open the eyes of the human and celestial realms and manifest the ancestral legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, you must further take this "self" and the "Field for Selecting Buddhas" [and examine them].
Melted into a single mass, it is cast far beyond hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds.
Turning back and shifting one’s steps, one travels all the way to the other side of Vīraśabda and even further, only to return and receive a severe blow from West Peak.
"O Great Assembly, since you have already cast it away for yourself, what is there left to receive the blow? Suddenly, there may be a man who disregards his very life.
"Disciple, had you heard such a presentation, you might have come forward, overturned the meditation seat, and dispersed the assembly; that would indeed have been so.
Nevertheless, West Peak Lion Rock has not yet granted its nod."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The realms of boundless lands do not separate self and other by even a hair’s breadth;
ten ages of past and present do not depart from the beginning and end within this very thought-moment.

It is just as when this mountain monk stays daily within Zhanggong Cave, sleeping horizontally or vertically, sometimes singing and sometimes chanting—do you all know this? Every day you are before the Field for Selecting Buddhas, walking east and west..."

Whether one acts with anger or joy, does the mountain monk still know this? If both parties know it, one cannot avoid being split into many bodies to be pounded in mortars, or having one’s tongue pulled out to be plowed by a bull.
If neither knows it, take it for granted that Śākyamuni will fold his hands in submission and Maitreya will take refuge [in you].
Why is this so? Have you not heard it said: "The single word 'knowing' is the gateway to all calamities"?
Ascending the hall: "The myriad dharmas return to the One. To what place does the One return? He then looked around left and right and descended from his seat. Ascending the hall:
"The entire world of the ten directions is this single alms bowl. You all eat gruel and rice within it; you defecate and urinate within it;
you walk, stand, sit, and lie down, even down to every movement and gesture—all is within it."
"Stillness! It is all contained within. If you can recognize it, even Master Bodhidharma would serve as nothing more than your foot-washing slave.
If you do not recognize it, with what will you eat your morning and evening gruel? Investigate!"
Ascending the hall on the first day of the New Year: At the beginning of the year, one carries out new ordinances. The pillar and the lantern—look quickly with your eyes and listen!
In the southwest corner of the hearth lies a square brick; it is alert and clever, clever and alert. Be mindful of this and dwell upon it;
be reverent and respectful. Why is this so? Because for Xu Shisanlang, this is his natal year and his destiny.

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "If you love someone, you wish them to live; if you hate someone, you wish them to die. These two layers of attachment to love and hate—[he strikes with his staff]—all arise from right here.
Even if you were to recognize the source, you would still have to buy straw sandals and travel for thirty years.
[He strikes with his staff. When has it ever trodden upon this very spot? He hurls down the staff and says: "If you have a staff..."
"Son, I give you this staff.
He ascends the hall, plants the staff on the ground, and says: "In the lion’s den, the lion roars; the lion’s cub has no before or after.
Suddenly, turning over in one fell swoop, he is able to open his mouth before others. Is there anyone here now who can turn over? He then hurls the staff down.
Zhaozhou said: "The shrimp leaps, yet cannot get out of the basket.

Regarding the opening of the retreat, he ascended the hall and said: "The great limit is ninety days; the small limit is seven days. Within the coarse there is the fine; within the fine there is the subtle."
Densely packed and without interval, not even a speck of dust can stand. At this very moment, it is like a silver mountain and an iron wall;
advancing, there is no door; retreating, one loses the way. It is as if falling into a ten-thousand-fathom deep pit, with precipices and thorns on all four sides.
You must be a fierce hero, determined to turn yourself around and leap out. If you hesitate for even a single thought, even a Buddha could not save you.
This is the most supreme gateway of the Mysterious Gate (Xuánmén). I universally exhort everyone to exert their strength.

Because of a realization gained from a Chan practitioner, I have been in the hall for over twenty years.

I have spread a vast net across the heavens to strike at phoenixes and snare dragons, yet I have never encountered so much as a single shrimp or crab. Today, unexpectedly, a tiny gnat has flown into the net;
though it is truly not fit to be looked upon, thirty years hence, atop a solitary peak and at the very summit, [it shall be seen].
He raised his voice and shouted loudly. But tell me, what did he shout? "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one sheet of snow.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Last night I composed a verse in a dream; let me recite it for the assembly. After a long pause, he said, "I have forgotten it.
Suddenly, he picked up his staff and said, "Does this staff remember? After another long pause, he said, "Those from the same pit are not different."

The Master ascends the hall for the Buddha-bath ceremony. He cites how, as soon as the World-Honored One was born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, walked seven steps, looked around in the four directions, and declared:
"In all the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored. The Master says: "To see a monster!"
There is nothing strange. That which is strange will destroy itself. Do you all understand? Listen further to this verse:

Pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, brandishing spears and halberds, The battle continues unabated until this very day. Even if all living beings were slaughtered to extinction, A single body would still have its own sorrows.
Ascending the hall to pray for clear weather: The celestial gate has long been locked and remains unopened; day and night, torrents pour down as black winds rage.

[He strikes the meditation seat once with his whisk and says: "With one blow of the mallet of indignant nature, everything is shattered to pieces; from the crown of the head, a single red orb bursts forth."
Ascending the hall in the Central Lands, [the Master] held up his whisk and said:

"If you can offer this before forty-five days have passed, it will not only consume ten thousand taels of gold daily, but will also be able to respond to the offerings of the four worlds. If you can offer this after forty-five days have passed—"
"Even for a single thread of silk or a drop of water, one must pull the plow and drag the harrow to repay them. Striking the meditation seat once with his whisk, he said:
"Having passed through the place where the gibbons cry out at Baxia, even one who is not a person of sorrow would break their heart."
Ascending the hall, he said: "I forgot the verse of the secret transmission from those years; In vain I have caused this assembly to endure such hardship.
Last night, upon my pillow, I suddenly remembered it: Every year in the fifth month, there is the plum blossom rain."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to the world; when a single speck of dust rises, the great earth is gathered up.
He gave a shout and said: "When there is spirit, add more spirit; where there is no elegance, there too is elegance."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The mud ox at the bottom of the sea chews the moon as it runs; the stone tiger before the cliff sleeps while cradling its cubs.

An iron snake drills into the diamond eye; the Kunlun man rides an elephant led by a heron. Within these four lines, there is one phrase that can kill and can bring to life, that can grant freedom and can seize.
If you can discern it, I grant that your lifelong study of Zen is complete."
Upon the arrival of Layman Zhigong, the Master ascended the hall and said: "I, this mountain monk, have a most extraordinary karmic connection that I have never before carelessly brought forth.

Today, fortunately meeting Layman Zhigong as my witness, I shall offer it to the great assembly. After a long silence, he said: "Delicious food does not satisfy the appetite of one who is already full."

Ascending the hall on the Winter Solstice: The Yin fades at the tip of the nose; The Yang arises from within the eyes. If you can grasp the meaning herein, You should continue your study for another thirty years.
Ascending the hall: Night after night, one embraces the Buddha in sleep; Morning after morning, one rises together with him. Qiu Yi Ji: as he rises and sits, [he is ever present].

Zheng followed him, transforming three thousand people. Whether speaking or remaining silent, they dwelt together; seventy scholars were never separated by even a hair’s breadth. You, young man, are like a shadow following a body.
As for the nine sons—if you wish to know where the Buddha dwells, O virtuous one, it is simply this sound of speech. This is what you should know.
Master Fu uttered these words with his voice, illuminating the past and soaring through the present; how wondrous! How sublime!
To add a point to the arrowhead is a laughable matter. A clever person, upon hearing it mentioned, grasps it like a pearl in the palm or fits a mustard seed into a needle’s eye.
If one’s faculties and thought are dull, they will fail three times without returning. Long ago, our Buddha, the World-Honored One...
Those of this sort may deliberate for twenty-one days until they have exhausted their calculations and forgotten their feelings, yet they cannot avoid collapsing body and soul.

They are far more than those who "swing a staff at the moon" or "join bamboo to point toward the sky. When the ancients offered a single word or half a phrase, it was like brandishing a sharp, polished blade.

It is like jade hidden within stone; those who recognize it know it to be a boulder of priceless value. Otherwise, it is nothing.

why wait until you stare with wide-open eyes, making gestures and setting patterns to look for a single character? If it were otherwise, the ancients said:
Do not say that "no-mind" is the Way; even no-mind still leaves one barrier behind. Not merely one barrier—know that there are hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions more.
If you do not rouse your resolve and apply yourself with diligent effort to this final stage of "dead-work," you will never succeed.
Is there any difference between wood and stone? When one’s practice reaches its ultimate limit, one must naturally enter the samādhi of no-mind;
yet this is fundamentally different from the "no-mind" of heaven and earth mentioned previously. As Bodhidharma said, "The mind is like a wall.
Confucius forgot the taste of food for three months, and Yan Hui remained as if ignorant all day long. Jia Dao engaged in deliberate selection and rejection through contemplation.

Reaching this point, that which can raise [the doubt] and that which is raised, that which can doubt and that which is doubted, are both forgotten and both extinguished; even non-existence is non-existent.

At eighteen, he studied the Tiantai teachings; at twenty, he changed his robes and entered Jingci Monastery.

It is clear. Look at how I have been wasting more than a year; every day I have been like a lost traveler.

At that time, being pressed by the three-year deadline, I was in the midst of great distress when I suddenly met my elder brother Jing from Taizhou, who said that Master Xueyan was constantly asking about my practice and why I had not gone to visit him. Thereupon, I joyfully took this to heart.

Xiang went to the head of the North Gorge Pagoda to seek instruction. Just as he was about to offer his greetings and insert incense, he was struck with a heavy, painful blow of the fist and driven out.
The door was immediately shut. He returned to the Sangha Hall, weeping all the way. The next day, after the morning gruel, he went up again and finally managed to approach him.
He asked about Xiang’s previous practice; Xiang confessed everything one by one, and was immediately granted the eradication [of his delusions] on that very spot.
Regarding the illnesses accumulated previously, have them instead contemplate the word "Mu" (無). Have them practice this method from beginning to end one full cycle;

He was like this today; he was like this tomorrow. Every day, as soon as [a student] entered, he would ask, "How is your practice going today?
Seeing that [the student] had made some progress, he eventually stopped asking about their specific practice.
As soon as someone entered the gate, he would ask, "Who brought this corpse here for you? Before the words were even finished, he would strike them with a powerful blow of his fist.

Every day, he would simply question him in this manner and strike him in this manner. Just as he was being pressed to the limit and a sense of boundary began to emerge, the Old Master received an invitation to go to Nanming.
Before departing, he instructed him, saying, "Once I have entered the monastery, I will send someone to fetch you.
However, no further news was heard. He then joined forces with his companion, Brother Ze from Changzhou, and they traveled together until they reached the home of a lay relative.
I packed my belongings. Unexpectedly, my lay relatives, considering that we were young and had never traveled before, confiscated all our luggage and ordination certificates.
It was the beginning of the second month, and I could find no place to register as a guest at various monasteries.

Having no choice, I carried my bundle up to Mount Jing and arrived at the Hall on the fifteenth day of the second month. Suddenly, on the night of the sixteenth of the following month, while in a dream...
I recalled the dialogue raised by Master Duanyao in his room regarding the saying, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return?
From that moment on, my state of doubt suddenly arose and coalesced into a single mass. I reached a point where I could no longer distinguish east from west and forgot both sleep and food.
On the sixth day, during the *chén-sì* period, while walking along the corridor, I saw the assembly of monks coming out from the hall; without realizing it, I rolled over into their ranks.
While he was reciting sutras atop the Three Pagoda Pavilion, he suddenly looked up and beheld the portrait eulogy of the Fifth Patriarch, Master Yuan.
The final two lines read: "In a hundred years, thirty-six thousand mornings; turning it over and over, it is always this very fellow.
Suddenly, the "sentence about dragging a corpse" that the Old Monk had questioned him with the day before broke apart within him. His soul flew and his heart turned cold with realization.
Upon his passing, he died and then revived once more; it was as if he had laid down a burden of one hundred and twenty catties.

This was the twenty-second day of the third month of the Xin-you year, the anniversary of the Shaolin Patriarch’s death. He was exactly twenty-four years old that year, having completed the three-year limit of training.

He then intended to travel south to Ming to seek a definitive resolution, but the summer retreat was approaching and the local villagers would not permit it. It was not until the conclusion of the retreat that he was allowed to go.

When it came time to speak, I felt inwardly that everything was muddled;

Unexpectedly, my fellow practitioner, Brother Ze, was bound for another mountain and suddenly departed from the Master’s presence.

It was not until the year Yichou (1805) that I was once again able to rely upon him when the Old Monk hung up the sign at the meditation hall; I followed him into service as we traveled to Tianning. During our stay there, I was subjected to an interrogation:
"In the midst of the vast activity of the day, are you still able to maintain your mastery? I replied, "I am able to maintain my mastery. Furthermore...
Question: "Can one maintain mastery while dreaming? Answer: "One maintains mastery. Question again:
"When one is fast asleep, without dreams and without thoughts, without seeing and without hearing—where is the master?
At this point, there was nothing left to say in response and no principle to be advanced. The Master then instructed him, saying: "From this day forward, you need not study the Buddha."
Regarding the study of the Dharma: do not seek it by poring over the past or the present. Simply eat when hungry and sleep when tired.
As soon as you wake from sleep, rouse your spirit and ask: "In what place does this master of mine ultimately reside and establish his life?
Although you may have sufficient faith and adhere to these words, alas, because your faculties are dull, you find yourself increasingly lost.

He then recalled the various points of confusion and contradiction that the Buddhas and patriarchs of the past had questioned.
Examination: The causes and conditions for the differences between ancient and modern times are precisely like seeing the Great Sage at Sizhou, or a traveler returning to his native village:
it is originally just that same person from before; one does not change the place where one formerly walked. From this point on, the state will be settled and the nation stabilized;
the world will enjoy peace. With a single thought of non-action, the ten directions are cut off. All that has been submitted above is entirely true. I prostrate myself.
I hope for your honored compassion; please deign to examine this in detail.

Why is it that the public cases of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are but a single principle, yet there are those who understand them and those who do not? Great practitioners...
People should follow the practice of the Buddha; why then do they not observe the *vinaya*? The bright sun is in the sky, illuminating everything;

He spoke universally. He regularly instructed people in the practice of investigating the koan: "The myriad dharmas all return to One; where does the One return?
When investigating, one must give rise to a great state of doubt: "All the myriad dharmas of the world return to a single dharma;

At the place of urination, rouse your spirit and act with urgency. Simply harbor this doubt: "Ultimately, where does it all return?
You must resolutely seek a clear understanding; do not cast it aside into a state of complacency, nor engage in random, distracted thoughts.

At the threshold of birth and death, it requires no words for one to understand: one must cause worldly sentiments and thoughts to become light and subtle; then, the thought of the Way will naturally grow profound.
As the ancients said: "That which is familiar must be made unfamiliar; that which is unfamiliar must be made familiar.

During leisure time, do not use the study of scriptures as a mere distraction; otherwise, your practice will fail to coalesce into a single whole. You must simply rise and practice the Way, applying your spirit with urgency.
Investigate where this "one" returns and where it settles. Naturally, there is no need to read sutras;
the *gong'an* itself is a continuous scroll of scripture that is constantly turned day and night. Why must you further add head upon head?
If you apply effort in this manner, the devas and nāgas will naturally protect and sustain you; there is no need for prayers. One simply needs to sever worldly ties and economize on speech.
An ancient said: "If for twenty years one does not open one's mouth to speak, even the Buddha will be unable to do anything with you later on.
The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. It is like people climbing a mountain: each must exert their own strength. Strive! A verse says:
Amidst the dust of the mundane world, one learns to dwell like a mountain hermit; when body and mind are stilled, the Way abounds.
Once all hatred and love within the breast are exhausted, even without practicing Chan, one’s cultivation is already lofty.

The *bhavāṅga* (the link of existence) remains. Since this is so, how should one act? "A bamboo shoots crookedly while pressed by a rock; flowers grow upside down while suspended from a cliff.

Only the old man did not withdraw. Baizhang asked, "Who are you? The old man replied, "Yes. I am no ordinary person.
In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, I once lived on this mountain. When a student asked me, 'Does one who practices great cultivation still fall within the realm of cause and effect?
I answered, 'He does not fall within cause and effect. Because of this, for five hundred lifetimes I have fallen into the body of a wild fox. Now..."

"Please, Preceptor, provide a turning word on my behalf so that I may be freed from this wild fox body. He then asked, "Does a person of great cultivation still fall within the realm of cause and effect?
Baizhang replied, "One does not obscure cause and effect. At these words, the old man attained great enlightenment.

He prostrated and said, "I have now been freed from the wild fox body; I dwell behind the mountain. I venture to request the Preceptor to allow me to be treated according to the rites for a deceased monk."
For example: After the meal, the Abbot ordered the *vinaya-dhara* (Rector) to strike the gavel and announce to the assembly that a deceased monk was to be escorted away.

The community discussed this, wondering why all were at peace and there were no other sick persons in the Nirvana Hall. Why was this so? After the meal, the Abbot personally led the assembly to the base of a cliff behind the mountain.
There, using a staff, he pried out the carcass of a dead wild fox and performed its cremation according to the Dharma.
The Master said, "Assembly, previously it was said 'not falling,' and later it was said 'not being obscured. Is there still gain and loss here or not?
If there is none, why is there falling and liberation? If there is, try bringing it forth and state it clearly.
Is there any? Is there any? You are all nothing but a pack of wild fox spirits. Do not take offense at this mountain monk for treating the noble as the lowly."
When the Tripitaka Master Mahakarṇa from the Western Heaven arrived at the capital, he claimed to have attained the supernormal power of knowing others' minds.
Emperor Suzong ordered National Teacher Zhong to test him. As soon as the Tripitaka Master saw Zhong, he prostrated and stood to the right.
Zhong asked, "Have you attained the power of knowing others' minds? The Tripitaka Master replied, "I dare not say so. Zhong said, "Tell me, where is this old monk right now? The Tripitaka Master—
Yangshan said, "The Master is the teacher of an entire nation. How can you go to West River to watch the boat races?

"How could you be watching a monkey perform on Tianjin Bridge? This was the third question posed by Huizhong. After a long while, the Tripitaka Master remained ignorant of where he had gone.
Huizhong rebuked him, saying, "You wild fox spirit! Where is your *paracittajñāna* (knowledge of others' minds) now? The Tripitaka Master was speechless.
The Master said: "Great as the National Teacher was, his lifelong skills were entirely exposed by this barbarian monk.
Nevertheless, it is fortunate that he encountered a sagely sovereign who provided witness."

If you wish to truly resolve your will and clarify the mind, first cast out entirely all the good and evil things that have accumulated within your chest during your daily life, leaving not even a hair’s breadth remaining.
Throughout the day, remain steadfast and vacant as if dull-witted, like an infant of old.

You must exhaustively investigate the profound mystery of the Ultimate Path and contemplate the secret intent of the West’s arrival. It is like a person traveling far to another land who gradually turns back on his path and arrives home;
or like a rat entering a cow’s horn that keeps running until it reaches the very tip and bottom;

or like catching a thief and demanding restitution until the matter is exhausted in both principle and circumstance—immovable and non-retreating, without going or coming, not a single thought arising, the past and future limits severed, standing firm and distinct.

It must simply be such that not even a speck of dust remains, not a blade of grass grows, coming and going without obstruction, and dwelling or departing with total freedom.

He thought to himself, "Where is my master? The Master remained silent. Qian instructed him, saying, "From this day forward, I shall not require you to study the Buddha or the Dharma.
Eat when hungry and sleep when weary; as soon as you awaken, shake off your lethargy and look—where exactly is the master of this moment?
The Master became even more alert and self-reflective. In the winter of the Bingyin year of the Xianchun era, he entered Longxu Mountain, where he slept upon wood and ate pine needles. The wind...

He struggled through the day in debate, vowing to reach a clear understanding in a single stroke. Five years passed. One night at midnight, as he pushed back his pillow, it fell to the floor with a sound;
he attained great enlightenment. At that time, heavy snow had cut off all roads for several days, and people said the Master was already gone.

When the snow cleared, he sat in meditation as before. In the year Jiashu, he moved to Mount Shuangji in Wukang. In the spring of the year Bingzi of the Deyou era, the Great Army arrived. The Master...
He fasted for nearly ten days, sitting upright without moving. Once the matter was settled, visitors arrived in great numbers, their shoes cluttering the doorway.

In the spring of the Ji-mao year, he retreated to Shiziyan on Mount Xitianmu, where he constructed a small chamber about one *zhang* square within a stone cave and inscribed it with the name "Deadman’s Barrier" (*Siguan*).
He completely discarded all attendants and finery; using a broken jar as a cauldron, he ate only once every two days. The cave was accessed by climbing a mountain ladder, so his disciples were few.
[They] built the Siṃhavana (Lion Garden) together to dwell in. He addressed the assembly with three "gateless barriers" (wuguan yu), saying:

"A person of ultimate penetration is fundamentally liberated from birth and death; why, then, is their life-root not severed? The public cases (gong'an) of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are but a single principle;
why, then, is there clarity and lack of clarity? A great practitioner of the Way should follow the conduct of the Buddha; why, then, do they not observe the Vinaya?"
Fuchi immediately barred the door and would not admit him. It happened that Huiqin had entrusted him with a bamboo whisk, a fly-whisk, and a dharma discourse; he took them out and offered incense.
His reputation for the Way grew daily, and those from distant regions and foreign lands came in succession to inquire about the Path. Qu Jingtfa, the Vice Commissioner of Yunsu, [resided at] Heisha.

He revered and admired the Master; upon seeing him once, their spiritual affinities were instantly harmonized. He immediately offered his fields and manor as a donation, but the Master declined and would not accept them.

The donor’s resolve to renounce became even firmer, so he had his disciples establish a separate monastery on the land for the purpose of providing sustenance. He selected a site called Lianhua, about ten *li* distant from the cliff.
He requested an official plaque for the temple, naming it Dajue Chan Temple (Great Enlightenment Chan Monastery), and appointed Zu Yong to oversee its affairs.

On the twenty-seventh day of the eleventh month of the year Yiwu, the Master suddenly wrote two scrolls of true calligraphy and entrusted them to Mingchu and Zu Yong as his final instructions. On the first day of the twelfth month, he ascended the hall and said:
"For thirty years on West Peak, I have vainly discoursed upon Prajñā; my offenses fill the heavens. As for this final phrase, I dare not [speak of it]."
"It involves the common people; I shall take it with me. "Great Assembly, is there anyone who knows where this falls? After a long silence, he said:
"A difference of a hair’s breadth, and heaven and earth are separated by a vast gulf. He then wrote another verse: "Coming, he did not enter the Death Barrier;
going, he did not exit the Death Barrier. An iron snake drills into the sea, knocking over Mount Sumeru. Thereupon he passed away peacefully. On the Gengshen day, his remains were enshrined.
His life was fully spent at the barrier of death. The Master was born on the twenty-third day of the third month in the Wuxu year of the Jiaxi era.

He lived to the age of fifty-eight and had been a monk for forty-three years. He had one hundred disciples, and those who received precepts or sought his instruction numbered in the tens of thousands from near and far, all hastening to him.

He burned incense at his arms and head, weeping bitterly until his throat was choked with sobs. His teacher Qingming was austere and simple in character, possessing a profound commitment to seeking the Way.

After attaining sudden enlightenment, he withdrew to dwell in a remote mountain, never venturing more than a few steps from his abode. With his inner mind free of agitation and his external ties to all conditions severed, he attained a state of joyful self-sufficiency.
He was supremely compassionate toward others, teaching them with earnest diligence; his speech was kind, gentle, and easygoing, often followed by tears when he entered their rooms.

Zhongxing Zu’s instructions were to whip and spur the dragon-elephants [of the mind], scrutinizing them with total sincerity and leaving no room for even a grain of negligence. He often cautioned his students:

"People today possess but a fragmentary understanding and cannot penetrate to the ultimate. When questioned by a fellow practitioner, they are utterly bewildered and unable to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
As phrases come and go, it is like a hand-clapping game with a child; this is because their realization is superficial and muddled. You must achieve a great, thorough penetration."

Having personally seen and realized this, he attained the wisdom of discernment (*viveka-jñāna*) and was finally able to examine and distinguish between "killing" and "giving life. His functional mastery was so steep and perilous that it could not be approached by ordinary means.
Even so, he remained particularly meticulous in his minor conduct and revered the precepts; though he founded two monasteries, his eyes never set foot within them.

The Master’s practice and realization were authentic; his fame resounded throughout the rivers and lakes. Whether they knew him or not, all placed their hands upon their foreheads and praised him, saying: "An ancient Buddha, a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
When I was in my early twenties, I studied under the Venerable Wuzhun; the Master was a grandson of Wuzhun.

He established monasteries and founded manors, twice entrusting me with the request for commemorative records. Since my mind has long since been subdued, how could I refuse the disciples who brought these accounts of his deeds and sought an inscription? Thus, I offer this epitaph.
It is said:
A high peak stands firm; from patriarch to descendant, the standard is one and the same. Seeking the Way in his prime, he accumulated true effort over time.
In the night of the empty mountains, as the sound of a staff striking the earth served as his pillow, the profound gate was suddenly flung open, and the universe was renewed.
The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? A phrase like "hot oil" makes the great earth dance;
the western peak’s gates are sealed in death. With thirty years remaining, he wraps his head in clouds and wears a snow-capped hat.
Friends come to his door, yet he is hung with not a single thread. Ten thousand fathoms high like a sheer wall—too near to moor upon, too far to approach.
Severing the lives of the patch-robed monks, Realizing the mind of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, With his hands he rends through heavy clouds; The moon clears over a thousand forests.
An iron serpent enters the sea, And empty space shatters into a hundred pieces. I compose this inscription poem; There is no sound of "being" or "non-being."
